items.title: @OpenAI：Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve re
items.abstract_or_text: Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications. On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments. While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software. After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

items.title: @pdhsu：Delighted to share a landmark preprint from our lab, using genome language models and AI agents for biological discovery
items.abstract_or_text: Delighted to share a landmark preprint from our lab, using genome language models and AI agents for biological discovery and genome mining! The stretches of DNA between protein-coding genes are often called the genome’s “dark matter,” but they are far from empty. They encode RNA molecules that sense metabolites, regulate genes, and control some of molecular biology's most important tools (such as programmable genome editors e.g. CRISPR/bridge). Much of this biology is unexplored. One reason is that RNAs can retain similar structures and functions even as their DNA sequences change dramatically, making their relationships difficult to recognize with conventional computational tools. To help map this territory, we finetuned a version of our genomic language model Evo 2 on bacterial and archaeal intergenic sequences, learning relationships between these regions even when they share little sequence similarity. We used it to organize 376 million intergenic sequences into COMPASS (COMPrehensive Atlas of Structured Sequences). Website: https://compass.arcinstitute.org/

items.title: @ClementDelangue：Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scientists, academia, non-p
items.abstract_or_text: Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scientists, academia, non-profits, health agencies,...) to use, study and understand it with widespread but shallow guardrails that the bad guys are bypassing easily. This is why we created Carbon-X, the best open-source DNA model by midtraining Qwen3-14B on 300B tokens of DNA, English and interleaved data. We also used a hybrid tokenizer that tokenizes English with BPE and DNA with a 6-mer tokenizer. As a result, Carbon-X outperforms all open language models we evaluated on five benchmarks of DNA understanding and generation. This is a 27-point improvement over Qwen3-14B. It is also API frontier level at 1,800x less cost than GPT 6.1 Sol!

items.title: @dair_ai：Great paper from Anthropic on AI agents doing ML-for-science research. They propose Agent4Sci, which gives frontier codi
items.abstract_or_text: Great paper from Anthropic on AI agents doing ML-for-science research. They propose Agent4Sci, which gives frontier coding agents 20 scientific ML benchmarks across 11 domains and asks them to beat the published best model. They beat it on all 20. Claude Opus improves on the published best by 10.4% on average, and no run was flagged for misconduct. Adding three lightweight skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raises Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%. The models stay the same, and the research scaffolding roughly doubles the gain.

items.title: @OpenAI：During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in
items.abstract_or_text: During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy. The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server. This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

items.abstract_or_text: New on our Frontier Red Team blog: using Claude to formally verify software at large scale. Formal verification can prove that code is free of certain bugs, but historically it has only been feasible for small codebases (or required a lot of expert time). With AI models, however, this is beginning to change. In collaboration with @theoremlabs, we used Claude to prove security properties in over one hundred real-world open-source libraries over the span of a few weeks.

items.title: @Math_files：A new NPR investigation has found a troubling problem in AI-generated mathematics. Cambridge mathematician Anders Hansen
items.abstract_or_text: A new NPR investigation has found a troubling problem in AI-generated mathematics. Cambridge mathematician Anders Hansen identified a discrepancy between an AI-generated proof and its Lean formalization. A constant had changed from 4 to 5, making the formally verified statement weaker than the original claim. The Lean verification itself was not necessarily incorrect. The concern is that it may have verified something different from what the original mathematical argument asserted. The investigation highlights a distinction that is becoming increasingly important: verifying a formal proof is not enough unless the formal statement faithfully represents the intended theorem. Source: NPR, 21 October 2026 (US), 22 October 2026 (IST).

items.abstract_or_text: OpenAI showed that AI agents can handle the slowest step in modern biology, making sense of huge experiments. By splitting a huge brain experiment among 1,946 AI agents, OpenAI got in 32 minutes what it estimates would take people months: a ranked list of leads for new brain-disease research. OpenAI, PerturbAI and Scripps Research had 1,946 GPT-Rosalind-5.5 agents interpret a whole-brain mouse CRISPR atlas in 32 minutes. They still matched or refined 48 of the 55 published findings the expression data could support.

items.abstract_or_text: This is one of the most interesting AI-for-research benchmarks I've seen recently. Huge congratulations to @MangQiuyang, @wenhaocha1, and the entire FrontierCS team! The design is particularly thoughtful. Take 48 published CS papers across 13 research areas, remove their key contributions from the original repositories, and ask AI agents to develop better solutions without access to the papers or the web. The strongest agent passes 58% of its runs, while none of the evaluated agents passes 16 of the 48 tasks.
